title: Ζεὺς καὶ ἄνθρωποι
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 120 (= Perry 108). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation ([ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ζεὺς πλάσας ἀνθρώπους ἐκέλευσεν Ἑρμῇ νοῦν αὐτοῖς ἐγχέαι.
sentences.tr: Zeus plasas anthrōpous ekeleusen Hermēi noun autois encheai.
sentences.l: Zeus, having moulded men, ordered Hermes to pour mind into them.
sentences.n: πλάσσω is the potter's word, of shaping figures out of clay — the standard Greek picture of the making of men. ἐγχέαι sets the governing image of the fable: mind is a liquid, poured and measured out.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος μέτρον ποιήσας ἴσον ἐνέχεεν ἑκάστῳ.
sentences.tr: Kakeinos metron poiēsas ison enecheen hekastōi.
sentences.l: And he, having made a measure, poured an equal one into each.
sentences.n: Κἀκεῖνος is καὶ ἐκεῖνος run together by crasis; the coronis over the alpha marks the coalescence, and ἐκεῖνος picks up Hermes. μέτρον is the measuring vessel itself, not the abstract quantity — a cup filled to the brim and emptied into each man alike.

sentences.t: Συνέβη δὲ τοὺς μὲν μικροφυεῖς πληρωθέντας τοῦ μέτρου φρονίμους γενέσθαι, τοὺς δὲ μακρούς, ἅτε μὴ ἐφικομένου τοῦ ποτοῦ [μηδὲ μέχρι γονάτων] εἰς πᾶν τὸ σῶμα, ἀφρονεστέρους γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr: Synebē de tous men mikrophyeis plērōthentas tou metrou phronimous genesthai, tous de makrous, hate mē ephikomenou tou potou [mēde mechri gonatōn] eis pan to sōma, aphronesterous genesthai.
sentences.l: And it came about that those of small growth, filled up with the measure, became sensible, while the tall ones, seeing that the drink did not reach [not even as far as the knees] into all the body, became the more senseless.
sentences.n: The square brackets are Chambry's: he prints μηδὲ μέχρι γονάτων but judges it interpolated and marks it for deletion. ἅτε with a genitive absolute gives the cause as a plain fact rather than as somebody's allegation. πληρόω takes the genitive of what a thing is filled with.

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα εὐμεγέθη μὲν σώματι, κατὰ ψυχὴν δὲ ἀλόγιστον ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros andra eumegethē men sōmati, kata psychēn de alogiston ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against a man of great size in body, but unreasoning in soul, the story is well-timed.
sentences.n: σώματι is a dative of respect — great in respect of body — and κατὰ ψυχήν does the same work with a preposition; μέν and δέ hold the two halves of the man apart. ἀλόγιστος is 'not reckoning', the man who does no calculating, which is what the fable says the tall were short of.
